newsitem.title: INDIA: India signs pact to control government borrowings.
newsitem.headline: India signs pact to control government borrowings.

text.p: India's Finance Ministry and central bank on Wednesday signed an agreement that would discipline fiscal spending by forcing the government to raise funds for its temporary cash needs at market interest rates.

Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor Chakravarti Rangarajan and Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia signed the agreement to introduce a new system of central bank funding to meet the government's borrowing needs in 1997/98 (April-March).
The new system would help the RBI control money supply and inflation fuelled by high state borrowings and make the government restrain spending in order to control its interest bill.
"I am happy this agreement has been reached," Rangarajan told a news conference after signing the pact in New Delhi.

Under the agreement, the government would no longer issue ad hoc treasury bills, used for four decades by the government to borrow funds at a fixed interest rate of 4.6 percent in order to meet unplanned cash needs.
Instead, a new system of ways and means advances (WMA) would control state borrowing through a limit on loans to the government.

Interest rates on such advances would attract market interest rates based on treasury bill auctions carried out by the central bank. Crossing the limits through overdrafts would attract even higher interest rates.

"The ad hocs...assumed in course of time a larger than life proportion posing a threat to monetary stability and the Reserve Bank's freedom of operating instruments of monetary policy for price stability," Rangarajan said in a statement.
The RBI is expecting to control money supply growth to 16 percent in 1997/98. Inflation based on wholesale prices, at 7.78 percent, was around 5.17 percent at the same time last year.

"The limit for ways and means advances will be 120 billion rupees ($3.35 billion) for the first half of the year (1997-98) (April-September) and 80 billion rupees ($2.23 billion) for the second half...," an RBI statement said.
Rangarajan said the limits referred to the maximum advances the government could have at any point to match temporary mismatches between government receipts and payments.

Up to the ways and means limit, the government would pay interest at 3.0 percentage points below the average yield rates on the cut-off prices at 91-day treasury bill auctions held in the previous quarter, the RBI statement said.
In 1997/98, for overdrafts beyond this limit, the rate would be 2.0 percentage points above the interest charged within the limit, the statement said.

"With overdrafts not being permitted beyond a period of 10 consecutive working days after March 1999, the scheme of WMA will culminate in an ideal position of fiscal balance being achieved," Rangarajan said.
The decision to conclude the agreement signed on Wednesday was announced by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his speech while presenting the budget for 1997/98 on February 28.
"WMA is not a source of financing and as such will not be shown as a source of financing the budget deficit," RBI said.
Ahluwalia said the new system would restrain fiscal spending but that did not mean a lack of flexibility. "Obviously there will be temporary mismatches," he said.
India aims to cut its fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997/98 from an expected 5.0 percent in 1996/97, and over the medium term cut the deficit to 3-4 percent.
